name: Exoplanet Atmosphere Spectroscopy
use: Reading the chemistry of planets around other stars
what: Working out which gases surround a planet orbiting another star from the starlight that passes through its atmosphere. JWST has detected carbon dioxide, water vapour and other molecules on exoplanets this way.
how: As the planet crosses its star, a thin ring of starlight filters through the atmosphere; each molecule absorbs specific infrared wavelengths, leaving a fingerprint in the spectrum.

name: Europa Clipper
use: Assessing whether an ocean moon could support life
what: NASA spacecraft launched in October 2024 to study Jupiter's moon Europa, which hides a salt-water ocean beneath its ice. It arrives in 2030 and will judge whether that ocean could be habitable.
how: Dozens of close flybys with ice-penetrating radar, a mass spectrometer, a dust analyser and cameras map the ice shell and sample material thrown up near the surface.

name: Habitable Worlds Observatory
use: Directly imaging Earth-like planets and searching them for life
what: NASA's planned flagship telescope for photographing Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars and searching their light for signs of life. It is in early design, targeted for the 2040s.
how: A large, ultra-stable space telescope with a coronagraph that suppresses the star's glare by around ten billion times, so the faint planet beside it can be seen and its spectrum taken.

name: Agnostic Life Detection
use: Recognising life that does not use DNA or proteins
what: Ways to recognise life without assuming it works like Earth life — for example by measuring how molecularly complex a sample is, on the proposal that complex molecules in abundance are very hard to make without biology.
how: Mass spectrometry scores molecular complexity (assembly theory proposes a threshold for this, and it is still debated); other approaches look for chemical disequilibrium or a strong left/right-handedness bias in molecules.

name: Extremophile Research
use: Mapping where life could survive on other worlds
what: Studying organisms that thrive in boiling vents, acid, ice, high radiation and deep rock. They set the known limits of life and so define which places on Mars, Europa or Enceladus are worth searching.
how: Sampling from Earth analogue sites — hydrothermal vents, Antarctic lakes, deep mines — followed by lab culturing and genome sequencing to find how each organism survives.

name: Technosignature Search (SETI)
use: Looking for evidence of technology beyond Earth
what: Searching for signs of technology elsewhere — radio beacons, laser pulses or industrial pollution — rather than biology. Breakthrough Listen is the largest such survey to date and has found no confirmed signal.
how: Radio telescopes scan millions of frequency channels for very narrow-band signals that natural sources do not produce; software filters out interference from Earth's own transmitters.

name: Exoplanet Transit Spectroscopy
what: Transmission spectroscopy now delivers molecular detections in exoplanet atmospheres at the micrometre level, including carbon dioxide, water, methane and sulphur dioxide. The method is the workhorse for deciding whether a world has a primary hydrogen envelope or a secondary, possibly rocky, atmosphere.
how: Starlight filtered through a planet atmosphere during transit carries absorption signatures; differencing in-transit against out-of-transit spectra isolates the planetary signal from the stellar one.

name: Habitable-Zone Planet Census
what: A curated catalogue of confirmed planets inside the conservative and optimistic liquid-water zones, used to prioritise follow-up spectroscopy and to estimate the frequency of temperate terrestrial worlds.
how: Radial-velocity and transit detections are combined with stellar luminosity models to compute incident flux, and planets are filtered by radius and equilibrium temperature.

name: PLATO Exoplanet Survey
what: A multi-camera space photometer designed to detect and characterise planets around bright, nearby stars, with particular sensitivity to Earth-size worlds in the habitable zone. Its seismology channel simultaneously ages the host stars.
how: An array of off-axis refracting telescopes images the same field, combining photometric precision with a very wide dynamic range for bright hosts.

name: ARIEL Atmospheric Survey
what: A dedicated survey observatory that will build a statistically meaningful sample of exoplanet spectra rather than studying single objects, enabling population-level conclusions about atmospheric diversity.
how: A passively cooled telescope feeding a spectrometer covers the near- and mid-infrared, using the host star as a calibration reference during every observation.

name: Microlensing Planet Survey
what: A wide-field infrared survey that uses gravitational microlensing to find planets at separations and masses that transit and radial-velocity methods cannot reach, including free-floating worlds.
how: A planet orbiting the lens star perturbs the magnification light curve; high-cadence infrared photometry from space resolves the perturbation against the Galactic bulge background.

name: Coronagraphic Direct Imaging
what: Ground-based extreme adaptive optics now images young, self-luminous giant planets and accretion disks around nearby stars, and measures their spectra and astrometry.
how: Thousands of actuators correct atmospheric turbulence in real time, then a coronagraph and post-processing algorithms subtract the residual stellar halo.

name: Extremely Large Telescope Imaging
what: A thirty-nine metre class segmented telescope that will deliver an order-of-magnitude gain in contrast and collecting area for direct characterisation of exoplanets and protoplanetary disks.
how: A segmented primary with integrated adaptive optics feeds high-resolution spectrographs, enabling spectral deconvolution of planet light from residual starlight.

name: Radio Technosignature Survey
what: A sustained, multi-telescope survey scanning nearby stars and the Galactic plane for narrowband radio emission inconsistent with any natural astrophysical process.
how: Digital signal processing searches terahertz of bandwidth for drifting narrowband carriers, and candidates are re-observed by an independent telescope to reject terrestrial interference.

name: FAST Radio Technosignature Search
what: The largest single-dish radio telescope in the world contributes unmatched raw sensitivity to narrowband technosignature searches, particularly for faint repeating signals.
how: A five-hundred-metre active spherical reflector with a deformable cable net focuses on a feed cabin, and multibeam receivers digitise wide bands for coherent dedispersion and drift searches.

name: SKA Technosignature Search
what: A low-frequency aperture array with enormous field of view and survey speed will execute commensal technosignature searches across the entire accessible sky during ordinary astronomy operations.
how: Thousands of dipole antennas form digital beams on the sky; beamformed voltage data is fed to dedicated search backends running simultaneously with the primary science correlator.

name: Optical SETI
what: Cherenkov telescopes repurposed for astrophysics also hunt nanosecond optical pulses, the signature of an artificial laser beacon that would outshine the host star by orders of magnitude.
how: Large photon-collecting mirrors with nanosecond-resolution photodetectors look for coincident multi-telescope triggers that rule out cosmic-ray-induced flashes.

name: Machine-Learning Technosignature Detection
what: Convolutional and transformer models trained on injected synthetic signals now classify candidate narrowband events, cutting the human review load on petabytes of survey data.
how: Spectrogram patches are labelled with simulated drifting carriers and real interference, then a supervised network ranks live candidates, with classical algorithms as a control.

name: Exoplanet Radio Emission Search
what: Low-frequency arrays attempt to detect coherent radio emission from star-planet interactions, which would directly measure an exoplanet magnetic field, a key shield for habitability.
how: Auroral cyclotron maser emission is predicted below a few hundred megahertz; long integrations and beamforming isolate the star system from confusion limits.

name: Radial-Velocity Precision Spectroscopy
what: Ultra-stable spectrographs on large telescopes now measure stellar reflex velocities at the metre-per-second level, supplying the masses that transit surveys cannot determine alone.
how: Light is dispersed across thousands of lines in a simultaneous reference channel; laser frequency combs or thorium-argon calibration track instrumental drift to centimetres per second.

name: Astrometric Planet Census
what: A whole-sky astrometric mission delivered precision parallaxes, proper motions and the first astrometric exoplanet detections, anchoring the mass-luminosity scale used by every other detection method.
how: Two telescopes scan the sky on a continuously changing angle, and global iterative solutions fit positions, parallaxes and orbital wobble simultaneously.

name: Exomoon Detection
what: Transit timing and duration variations are now used to test for moons and trojan companions around transiting planets, a discipline that would expand the habitable real estate of known systems.
how: A moon induces small periodic offsets in transit centre time and duration; long-baseline photometry plus transit-shape modelling recovers the perturbation against stellar noise.

name: Atmospheric Retrieval Pipelines
what: Bayesian and neural retrieval codes invert spectra into temperature profiles, molecular abundances, cloud decks and limb darkening, including rigorous false-positive accounting.
how: Radiative transfer forward models are sampled with nested sampling or simulation-based inference to produce posterior distributions over atmospheric parameters.

name: Venus Cloud Chemistry
what: Detections and non-detections of phosphine and sulphur species in the Venusian cloud deck have driven a rigorous re-examination of whether the middle cloud layer could host microbial life.
how: Ground-based and orbital spectroscopy of Venusian atmospheric windows is combined with photochemical models that test whether observed abundances require an unknown source.

name: Mars Methane Monitoring
what: Two independent spacecraft measure methane and its isotopic ratios at Mars, constraining whether episodic releases are geological, biological or instrumental artefacts.
how: Laser heterodyne and infrared solar occultation spectrometry resolve methane, ethane and carbon isotopes at parts-per-trillion levels from orbit and from the surface.

name: JUICE Icy Moon Tour
what: A European spacecraft in cruise phase will enter orbit around Ganymede after flybys of Callisto and Europa, carrying the most complete remote-sensing payload yet sent to the Jovian system.
how: Ice-penetrating radar, laser altimetry, magnetometry and submillimetre spectrometry are combined to infer ocean depth and detect internal liquid layers.

name: Dragonfly Titan Rotorcraft
what: A nuclear-powered rotorcraft will hop between sites on Titan, sampling prebiotic surface chemistry across hundreds of kilometres rather than at a single landing point.
how: Eight rotors allow multi-kilometre flights in the dense low-gravity atmosphere; a mass spectrometer and chemical analyser characterise organics at each landing site.

name: ExoMars Rosalind Franklin Rover
what: A rover with a two-metre drill will sample Martian subsurface material shielded from radiation and oxidants, the most favourable environment for preserved organic molecules.
how: A rotary-percussive drill extracts cores from beneath the oxidised layer; a mass spectrometer and Raman instrument then analyse them inside a sealed laboratory.

name: Venus Life Finder
what: A series of small, low-cost probes designed to descend through the Venusian cloud deck and measure organic chemistry and droplet composition directly, rather than spectroscopically.
how: A compact entry vehicle carries a fluorescence-based organic detector and a cloud-particle analyser, using a small dedicated launch vehicle to keep mission cost low.

name: Uranus Orbiter and Probe
what: The highest-priority planetary flagship concept will place an orbiter and an atmospheric entry probe at Uranus, sampling primordial composition preserved since solar system formation.
how: The orbiter carries magnetometry, a Narrow-angle imager and mass spectrometry; the probe descends under a parachute transmitting composition data before the pressure and heat kill it.

name: Enceladus Orbilander
what: A proposed mission that would both orbit and land at Enceladus, collecting fresh plume material ejected from its subsurface ocean and analysing it for biosignature patterns.
how: Plume flyby sampling at kilometres per second is followed by a landing phase that collects fall-out material and runs life-detection instruments directly on ocean-derived ice.

name: Cryobot Subsurface Ocean Access
what: Thermal and hybrid melting probes are being developed to descend through kilometres of ice shell and reach liquid water directly, the only way to verify ocean habitability in situ.
how: A nuclear or radioisotope heat source melts a descending borehole, with a tether carrying power and data; hybrid designs add a mechanical cutting head for debris layers.

name: Ice-Penetrating Radar Sounding
what: Low-frequency radar sounders on planetary spacecraft map internal ice layering, basal topography and the presence of liquid water beneath ice shells and polar caps.
how: Radar waves penetrate ice with low loss and reflect from dielectric contrasts at the ice-water or ice-rock interface, with coherent processing resolving depth.

name: Biosignature False-Positive Framework
what: A structured standard for deciding which atmospheric detections can reasonably be called biosignatures, requiring abiotic explanations to be explicitly quantified before any claim is made.
how: A catalogue of known abiotic production pathways and photochemical models is applied to each candidate spectrum, and the surviving explanatory gap is reported rather than the raw detection.

name: Space-Radiation Extremophile Survivability
what: Long-duration exposure platforms outside spacecraft test whether spores, lichens and biofilms survive vacuum, ultraviolet and cosmic radiation, directly bounding panspermia and forward-contamination risk.
how: Samples are mounted on external facility trays with dosimetry and are returned for viability assays; organic degradation is tracked spectroscopically in parallel.

name: Hydrothermal Vent Origin-of-Life Chemistry
what: Laboratory reactors reproducing alkaline hydrothermal vent conditions generate organic molecules and proton gradients without enzymes, the leading candidate for the energy source of the first metabolism.
how: Microfluidic and high-pressure reactors precipitate iron-sulphide membranes across a pH gradient and drive carbon fixation and phosphorylation chemistry.

name: Interstellar Probe Mission
what: An interstellar probe is a fast, lightweight spacecraft aimed past the heliosphere to sample the local interstellar medium directly, rather than inferring it from remote sensing. It is the first mission class designed to leave the Sun's influence while still returning data.
how: The architecture combines a radioisotope power source, a high-gain antenna for communication across hundreds of astronomical units, and a trajectory that uses a Jupiter gravity assist or a solar Oberth manoeuvre. Transit to the heliopause takes decades, so instrument autonomy and power longevity dominate the design.
companies: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory

name: Solar Gravitational Lens Telescope
what: A spacecraft parked in the solar gravitational focal region uses the Sun itself as an optical lens with an effective aperture of roughly a million kilometres. That gain is enough in principle to resolve surface features on an exoplanet tens of light years away.
how: Light from a distant system is bent by solar gravity and converges along a focal line extending outward from about 550 astronomical units, where a modest telescope collects it. The image arrives as an Einstein ring that must be computationally inverted, and the spacecraft must be navigated precisely at an enormous distance from Earth.

name: Enceladus Plume Sampling
what: Enceladus vents its subsurface ocean directly into space as plumes, so a spacecraft can sample ocean material without landing or drilling. It is the only known place where an ocean world delivers its chemistry to a passing probe.
how: A mission would either fly repeatedly through the plume at high velocity collecting ice grains, or land near a vent and collect fresh fallout, then analyse it with mass spectrometry and, in some architectures, return a sample to Earth. Plume encounter velocity and contamination control are the main design constraints.
companies: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory

name: Lightsail Interstellar Precursor
what: A laser-driven lightsail array would accelerate hundreds of gram-scale probes to a fraction of light speed for flyby reconnaissance of the nearest stars. It is the only architecture that reaches another system within a human lifetime using near-term physics.
how: A ground-based phased laser array pushes a metre-scale sail for several minutes, after which the probes coast, and a small fraction reach the target system and transmit data back with a compact laser or radio link. Atmosphere turbulence, sail survivability and the enormous receiver aperture needed for the return signal are the open problems.

name: Transmission Spectroscopy
what: Transmission spectroscopy reads the atmosphere of a transiting exoplanet by analysing starlight that has passed through its limb. It is the workhorse technique that turned exoplanet atmospheres from speculation into measurement.
how: During transit, molecules in the planet's atmosphere absorb specific wavelengths, imprinting a subtly deeper absorption feature at those bands and making the planet appear slightly larger at those colours. Separating that signal from stellar activity and instrument systematics is the central difficulty.

name: Coronagraphy and Starshade
what: Coronagraphy blocks a star's light inside the telescope to reveal faint companions, while a starshade flies tens of thousands of kilometres ahead as an external occulter. Together they enable direct imaging and spectroscopy of planets rather than indirect inference.
how: An internal coronagraph uses deformable mirrors and shaped pupils to suppress diffracted starlight, and a starshade blocks the star before light enters the aperture, removing diffraction at source. Both demand wavefront stability at the picometre level and precise formation flying in the starshade case.

name: Subsurface Ocean Radar Sounding
what: Low-frequency radar penetrates kilometres of ice and reflects from the boundary between ice and liquid water, mapping the shape of subsurface oceans and detecting internal lakes. It is the primary tool for finding liquid water without landing.
how: Radar pulses at wavelengths of tens of metres pass through ice with little loss but reflect strongly at a water interface, and the delay and strength of the echo give depth and interface properties. Ionospheric distortion and surface clutter must be modelled out before the deep echo can be identified.

name: Extremophile Biology
what: Extremophiles define the actual envelope of life on Earth, including organisms that thrive in boiling vents, acid mine drainage, radiation fields and deep subsurface rock. Their limits are the best available proxy for where life might exist elsewhere.
how: Culture-independent sequencing, metagenomics and high-pressure or high-radiation laboratory experiments establish which metabolisms and biomolecules survive which conditions. The findings feed directly into planetary protection rules and instrument design for life detection.

name: Hydrothermal Chemosynthesis
what: Hydrothermal vent ecosystems run on chemical energy rather than sunlight, with microbes oxidising hydrogen sulphide, methane and hydrogen to fix carbon. They demonstrate that a biosphere does not require a star's light, only a chemical gradient.
how: Fluid circulating through hot rock reacts with minerals and emerges reduced, and chemolithoautotrophs harvest the disequilibrium between that fluid and seawater. The same redox chemistry is the leading candidate for life in Europa and Enceladus oceans.
